summary:
Jeffrey Lee-Chan shares his production AI agent harness called Open Claw for developing at idea velocity. The talk opens with workshop logistics for both new and advanced users, including help with installation and an experimental dual-Open-Claw staging environment. Jeffrey describes his core setup: when everything works (~70% of the time), you describe tasks in brief Slack-like messages and Open Claw leverages persistent context and memory to understand references without re-explanation. He uses multiple agents with git work trees for parallelization and CI code integration. He notes his responses are simple enough that an agent could eventually replace him, motivating his push toward greater autonomy.

Key architectural concepts include frictionless communication (easily talking to AI vs. remote desktop) and a central axis—a spectrum from cowboy mode giving agents act permissions to fully managed agents. Open Claw uses agent orchestrator managers that supervise workers. Jeffrey uses tmux terminals for personal control and a forked open-source framework called agent orchestrator for workers. Once reaching Claude code, workers can spawn sub-agents autonomously.

The critical specialization insight: Open Claw decisions focus on spec, goals, and task history rather than implementation details. When using Claude directly, approximately 25% of context is consumed by implementation details (Claude MDs, skills, MCPs). Open Claw separates these concerns so managers reason about what to do, not how.

Jeffrey demonstrates two production websites: an AI RPG with a D&D dice system building custom reactive worlds, and a multi-AI analysis tool querying multiple models and synthesizing answers with vertical tabs and notifications. A key benefit of the manager role is reducing implementation bias—managers with different context provide more objective PR assessments than workers biased toward claiming success. Austin, a tmux creator, presents Cmux features including Cloud Code Teams integration and Cmux SSH for remote work.

The final Q&A explores dual staging environments—one instance for local development and another for integration testing on sandbox—increasing token usage but improving reliability before production deployment. Jeffrey shares model selection strategy: he uses Codex 53 as his orchestrator model, finding GPT 54 consumes more tokens, and switches to MiniMax when token budget runs low for cost management rather than preference.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Workshop logistics & setup overview
sections.summary: Jeffrey covers workshop structure for new and advanced users. He describes his core setup: ~70% first-run success, brief Slack-like messages leveraging persistent context, multiple agents with work trees for parallelization, CI integration, and brief debugging interactions. He notes his responses are simple enough that an agent could replace him, motivating autonomy work.

sections.title: Open Claw concepts & architecture
sections.summary: Introduces Open Claw concepts: frictionless communication, central axis (spectrum from cowboy mode to managed agents), agent orchestrator managers supervising workers, tmux for personal control, and a forked agent orchestrator framework. Managed agents run Claude code which can spawn sub-agents autonomously.

sections.title: Q&A: Open Claw vs Claude specialization
sections.summary: Explains why Open Claw over direct Claude: specialization. Open Claw decisions focus on spec, goals, and task history rather than implementation details. Direct Claude usage consumes ~25% of context on implementation (Claude MDs, skills, MCPs). Discusses testing pyramid: unit tests, MCP/JSON tests, browser/visual tests. Notes agents improved at browser tests over 6-12 months.

sections.title: Website demonstrations
sections.summary: Demonstrates an AI RPG with D&D dice mechanics building custom reactive worlds, and a multi-AI analysis tool that queries multiple models and synthesizes answers with vertical tabs and notifications for workflow management.

sections.title: Manager bias reduction & tmux/Cmux features
sections.summary: Discusses how the manager role reduces implementation bias—managers with different context provide objective PR assessments vs workers biased toward success. Austin from tmux presents Cmux features: Cloud Code Teams integration auto-spawning terminals, Cmux SSH for remote work. Concludes with sandbox discussion for model testing.

sections.title: Q&A: Dual staging setup & model selection
sections.summary: Jeffrey discusses the experimental dual-Open-Claw staging environment: one instance for local development, another for integration testing on sandbox, increasing token usage but improving reliability before production deployment. He shares model selection strategy: using Codex 53 as orchestrator (GPT 54 found to use more tokens), switching to MiniMax when token budget runs low for cost management rather than preference.
